DECISION 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
SUMMARY 
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority or PURA) allocates 
$1,988,010.51 in grants from the Public, Educational and Governmental Programming 
and Education Technology Investment Account (PEGPETIA). The Authority awards 
PEGPETIA funds accumulated through February 28, 2025, in this proceeding, with 
$995,132.19 for 33 grants to support public, educational, and governmental programming 
(PEG Grants) and $992,878.32 for 81 grants to support educational technology initiatives 
(ETI Grants). 
B. 
BACKGROUND OF THE PROCEEDING 
In 2007, the General Assembly established the PEGPETIA program to promote 
and improve public, educational, and governmental programming and to support 
education technology initiatives. See Public Act No. 07-253, § 33, codified as General 
Statutes § 16-331cc. The program is funded by a quarterly tax on the gross earnings of 
video service providers. General Statutes § 16-331cc. 
Since 2022, the Authority has conducted annual proceedings to determine the 
allocation of accumulated funding in the account and to administer grants to eligible 
entities. The Authority established the application requirements through a contested 
proceeding in 2008 and revised the requirements in 2019. Decision, Mar. 26, 2008, 
Docket No. 07-10-11, DPUC Proceeding to Establish Administrative Guidelines for the 
Public Educational and Governmental Programming and Educational Technology 
Investment Account Pursuant to Public Act 07-253 (Guidelines Decision); Decision, Oct. 
23, 2019, Docket No. 07-10-11RE01, DPUC Proceeding to Establish Administrative 
Guidelines for the Public Educational and Governmental Programming and Education 
Technology Investment Account – Grant Eligibility Criteria and Guidelines (Revised 
Guidelines Decision); General Statutes § 16-331cc(d); Corresp., Nov. 20, 2019, Docket 
No. 19-11-01, Public Educational and Governmental Programming and Education 
Technology Investment Account Program Pursuant to Public Act 07-253 (PEGPETIA 
Educational Grant Guidance). 
C. 
CONDUCT OF THE PROCEEDING 
On September 1, 2024, the Authority issued a Notice of Proceeding, which notified 
prospective applicants that all grant applications must be submitted by February 28, 2025. 
The Authority received a total of 136 applications, filed as motions, during the 
application window, September 1, 2024, through February 28, 2025. 
The Authority issued a proposed final decision in this matter on March 21, 2025. 
All participants were given the opportunity to file written exceptions to the proposed final 
decision. One participant also filed an objection to another participant’s application. 
D. 
PARTICIPANTS 
A list of participants is attached as Appendix A. 

Docket No. 24-10-02 
Page 2

II. 
AUTHORITY ANALYSIS 
A. 
INTRODUCTION 
In this proceeding, the Authority awards $1,988,010.51 of PEGPETIA funds 
accumulated through February 28, 2025.1 The Authority awards 50% of PEGPETIA grant 
funding to: (1) local community antenna television and video advisory councils; (2) the 
state-wide video advisory council; (3) public, educational, and governmental 
programmers; and (4) public, educational, and governmental studio operators, “to 
subsidize capital and equipment costs related to producing and procuring [public, 
educational, and governmental] programming.” General Statutes § 16-331cc(b). The 
Authority awards the remaining 50% of PEGPETIA grant funding “to boards of education 
and other education entities for education technology initiatives.” Id. 
B. 
USE OF PEGPETIA GRANT FUNDS 
1. PEG Grant Permissible Uses 
PEG Grant funds must be used for capital and equipment costs that aid the 
production or procurement of public, educational, and governmental programs for use on 
a cable television channel. PEG Grant funding is intended to promote and improve public, 
educational, and governmental access programming in Connecticut. Guidelines 
Decision, p. 2. Although funds are available to a wide variety of entities involved either 
directly or indirectly in producing community access programs, the awarding of funds to 
those entities is not the goal of the program. Id. The goal of PEG Grant funding is to 
“increase the quantity, quality and variety of community access productions made 
available to Competitive Video Service Providers (CVSP) and Community Antenna 
Television (CATV2) subscribers.” Guidelines Decision, p. 2. 
In each franchise area in Connecticut, a company or organization may be selected 
to assume responsibility for community access operations. General Statutes § 16-
331a(b)–(c). “Each franchise holder3 shall maintain at least one specially designated 
channel to be used for community access.” Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-2(a). The 
Authority has defined the term Community Access Provider (CAP) as “the entity 
responsible for providing community access operations within a franchise area.” Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-1(1). Each CAP is required to provide “facilities, equipment, 
and technical and managerial support to enable the production of meaningful community 
access programming within [each] franchise area. Each company shall include all its 
community access channels in its basic service package.” General Statutes § 16-
331a(b). “Community access” means public access, educational access and 

1 Simsbury Community Media submitted a written exception to the proposed final decision on March 27, 
2025, requesting the Authority verify the amount of funding available for distribution in this grant cycle. 
The Authority identified a small increase in available funds, which is reflected in the grant awards 
discussed below. Although more deposits appear to have been made to the PEGPETIA fund in recent 
months, those funds are not presently available to the Authority for disbursement. All funds collected will 
continue to accrue, however, and available funds will be disbursed in the next PEGPETIA grant cycle. 
2 “‘CATV’ means any system operated in, under or over any street or highway for the purpose of providing 
community antenna television service for hire pursuant to a certificate of public convenience and 
necessity issued by” PURA. Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-333-1(1). 
3 “‘Franchise holder’ means the holder of a certificate of public convenience and necessity to construct or 
operate a community antenna television system issued by” PURA. Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-333-1(8). 

Docket No. 24-10-02 
Page 3

governmental access.” Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-333-31(6). “Public access refers to 
the use of a cable television channel for non-commercial programming by any person.” 
Conn. Agencies Regs. § 16-333-31(2). “‘Educational access’ means the use of a 
community access channel for non-commercial educational programming.”4 Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-333-31(4). “‘Governmental access’ means the use of a community 
access channel for non-commercial governmental programming.” Conn. Agencies Regs. 
§ 16-333-31(5). 
Accordingly, PEG Grant funds must be used for capital and equipment costs that 
aid the production or procurement of public, educational, and governmental programs for 
broadcast on Connecticut community access channels.5 After receiving a PEG Grant, 
recipients must file a report with the Authority, stating: (a) the title, subject, and duration 
(in minutes) of all community access programs facilitated in whole or in part by the grant 
award; (b) how the programs were distributed through community access channels; and 
(c) the protocols for ensuring that any programs produced with equipment purchased with 
PEGPETIA funds are made available to the applicant’s local PEG studio.6 
Awarded PEG Grant funds may be applied toward expenses related to any capital 
and investment project listed in the application that aid the production or procurement of 
public, educational, and governmental programs for broadcast on Connecticut community 
access channels, with less than 10% used for non-equipment costs.7 
This year, as in years past, the Authority received written exceptions urging the 
disqualification of certain applicants because they are faith-based organizations. See, 
e.g., WPAA Written Exceptions, p. 2 (“What was once equal eligibility of the people for 
distribution of beliefs appears to be direct underwriting of faith-based organizations in a 
manner that enables worship, prayer, proselytizing, or devotional study. According to a 
common understanding of the separation of church and state, grants for video equipment 
for churches should not be happening.”) (emphasis in original). Because of the 
persistent misunderstanding of the concept of the “separation of church and state” 
doctrine, the Authority reminds participants that the allocation of funding is made for 
capital and equipment costs that aid the production or procurement of public, educational, 
and governmental programs for broadcast on Connecticut community access channels. 
The Authority neither endorses nor discriminates against producers of public, educational, 

4 “‘Educational programming’ means programming generally considered to be educational in scope and in 
content, or provided by private independent educational programming producers, and any educational 
programming transmitted over public access channel provided by the franchise holder.” Conn. Agencies 
Regs. § 16-333-1(14). 
5 The Authority maintains a list of Connecticut public access channels and studios at https://portal.ct.gov/-

22.pdf?rev=525f4ceb5f1b4258ab039cb1bb05bd97&hash=5040F0AAFCFFDDD568207FB9A84624E6. 
6 There is no prohibition on making PEG programming available in other formats, including online 
streaming, but funding must be used principally to produce programs that will be submitted for broadcast 
on Connecticut community access channels. 
7 Costs that are ineligible for PEGPETIA funding include expenses for permitting, travel, lodging, and 
salaries. See Guidelines Decision, pp. 3–4. PEGPETIA grant funds may not be used on non-equipment 
costs such as salaries, service agreements, or stipends. Non-equipment costs, such as design and 
engineering, installation, training, warranties, or insurance, must be reasonable and should be limited to 
less than 10% of the overall grant, unless an explanation is provided in the application. Software may be 
categorized as equipment, however.

and governmental programming on the basis of religious belief or religious speech. The 
Authority is only charged with allocating funding to improve the quantity and quality of 
content produced and not with choosing which speech is favored. 
2. ETI Grant Permissible Uses 
ETI Grant funding is intended to support education technology initiatives of boards 
of education and other education entities. General Statutes § 16-331cc(b) provides that 
half of PEGPETIA funds “shall be available to boards of education and other education 
entities for education technology initiatives.” Accordingly, ETI Grant funds should be used 
to support education technology initiatives of boards of education and other education 
entities. 
The term “education technology initiatives” is not defined in by General Statutes § 
16-331cc. In the Guidelines Decision, the Authority’s predecessor stated: 
The Department also believes that by including the phrase “education 
technology investment fund” in the definition of the account, the 
Legislature’s goal is to increase the quantity, quality and variety of 
educational programming currently being produced in Connecticut by 
public, educational and government studios, boards of education and other 
educational entities. 
Guidelines Decision, pp. 2–3. 
Subsequently, however, the Authority considered “term ‘education technology 
initiatives’ as it is used in [General Statutes] § 16-331cc(b) regarding the allocation of 
grant funds” in response to inquiries. PEGPETIA Educational Grant Guidance, p. 1. The 
Authority noted that it had not previously addressed the issue and offered the following 
guidance: 
The term “education technology initiatives” is not defined in the PEGPETIA 
statute, but the General Assembly has expressed its understanding of 
education technology through Chapter 61a of Title 4d of the General 
Statutes, which is entitled “Education Technology” and establishes a 
committee to implement state-wide education technology goals. In 
particular, under [General Statutes] § 4d-80(c)(2), the General Assembly 
articulated the following education technology goals: 
(A) Connecting all institutions of higher education, libraries, public 
elementary and secondary schools, regional educational service centers 
and other parties through a state-wide high speed, flexible network that will 
allow for video, voice and data transmission; 
(B) Wiring all school classrooms and connecting them to the Internet and to 
the state-wide high speed network through wired, wireless, or any other 
digital transmission technology providing high speed connectivity; 
(C) Providing access for all public schools, public libraries and libraries at 
institutions of higher education to a core set of on-line full text resources 

Docket No. 24-10-02 
Page 5

and to the ability to purchase collaboratively for other collections in order to 
maximize buying power; 
(D) Ensuring, in cooperation with the State Board of Education, competency 
in computing skills by the sixth grade for all students; 
(E) Ensuring competency in specific computing skills and the integration of 
technology into the curriculum for all public school teachers; and 
(F) Ensuring that institutions of higher education offer a wide range of 
course and degree programs via the Internet and through other 
synchronous and asynchronous methods. 
In addition, the Commission for Education Technology (CET) has issued a 
number of reports and guidance documents. On June 26, 2017, the CET 
released its “State Education Technology Goals and Plan, 2017–2022.” In 
the plan, the CET identified three core focus areas of (1) digital learning, (2) 
infrastructure, and (3) data and privacy. 
In light of these expressly stated goals and core focus areas related to 
education technology, the Authority will interpret the term “education 
technology initiatives” as applying to projects that advance or are consistent 
with at least one of these goals or focus area 
PEGPETIA Educational Grant Guidance, pp. 1–2. 
Awarded ETI Grant funds may be applied toward the expenses related to any 
capital expense listed in the application that will support those educational technology 
goals, with less than 10% used for non-equipment costs.8 To ensure the funding is used 
appropriately, ETI Grant recipients must file a report of the project enabled by the grant 
funds after completion of the project. 
3. Unused funds 
Any unused funds must be returned to the DEEP Business Office by May 15, 2026. 
If a grant recipient does not return unused funds, the recipient may be ineligible to receive 
all or part of future grant awards. 
C. 
APPLICATION PROCESS AND ELIGIBILITY REVIEW 
On September 3, 2024, the Authority provided access to the Application and 
Itemized Budget Forms in this docket, the docket schedule, and a website with detailed 
instructions regarding the application process, deadlines, and frequently asked question.9 
On September 3, 2024, the Authority issued a notice of a Question and Answer (Q&A) 
Session scheduled for October 24, 2024. The agenda for the Q&A Session was issued 
on October 21, 2024, and included a list of the deadlines for compliance in Docket No.

applications. On October 28, 2024, the Authority issued correspondence reiterating those 
dates and including 28 PowerPoint Slides explaining the application process and 
summarizing answers to questions from the Q&A Session. 
In this docket, 136 applications were submitted, including 46 applications for PEG 
Grants and 90 applications for ETI Grants. Following a review of those applications, the 
Authority awards 33 PEG Grants and 81 ETI Grants to eligible applicants. 
Several grant applicants submitted revised application materials as written 
exceptions. As discussed in Section II.D, below, below, however, applicants were 
responsible for ensuring their application materials were accurately completed and 
submitted before March 7, 2025. Application materials provided after that date were not 
considered for eligibility in this grant cycle. 
Although the Authority is sympathetic to the disappointment of ineligible applicants, 
it is important to the integrity and efficiency of this proceeding that all applicants abide by 
the noticed deadlines and provide the Authority and other docket participants with 
required information in a standardized format. 
D. 
INELIGIBLE APPLICANTS 
1. Incomplete Applications 
As a courtesy, Authority staff contacted dozens of applicants, as applications were 
received, with notice of deficiencies in their application packages, including failure to use 
the required forms, failure to properly complete and sign the required forms, and failure 
to provide the required supporting documentation. Several applicants also failed to 
provide timely compliance in prior dockets.11 Notably, despite an application window of 
nearly six full months, 86 of the 136 applications were filed within 5 days of the application 
deadline, with 47 filed on or after the last day of the application window. As a result, many 
applicants failed to complete their application before the deadline of March 7, 2025.12

E. 
ALLOCATION OF PEGPETIA FUNDS 
1. Total Grant Allocation 
In total, the Authority awards $995,132.19 for 33 PEG Grants and a total of 
$992,878.32 for 81 ETI Grants to eligible applicants. The Authority awards half of the 
funding in PEG Grants for capital and equipment costs related to producing and procuring 
public, educational and governmental programming, and the Authority awards half of the 
funding in ETI Grants for education technology initiatives. General Statutes § 16-
331cc(b). PEG Grants are available to (1) local community antenna television and video 
advisory councils, (2) the state-wide video advisory council (3) public, educational, and 
governmental programmers, and (4) public, educational, and governmental studio 
operators. Id. ETI Grants are available to boards of education and other education 
entities. Id. 
The Authority received 136 applications for PEGPETIA grants, with 22 applicants 
deemed wholly ineligible. The 33 eligible PEG Grant applicants sought a total of

$2,954,471.75 for public, educational, and governmental programming. The 81 eligible 
ETI Grant applicants sought $8,791,205.72 for education technology initiatives. 
To allocate the funding available for PEG and ETI Grants to all eligible applicants, 
the Authority applied a cap of $49,000 on PEG Grants for public access studios, a cap of 
$10,000 on PEG Grants for other PEG programmers, a cap of $17,000 on ETI Grants for 
libraries, and a cap of $12,000 on ETI Grants for boards of education and other 
educational entities. 
2. PEG Grant Allocation 
For this grant cycle, the Authority has capped funding for PEG studios at $49,000 
and for PEG programmers at $10,000. In the Revised Guidelines Decision, the Authority 
noted the problems inherent in providing PEG Grant funding to individuals. See Revised 
Guidelines Decision, p. 2 (recognizing “the value that individuals may bring to community 
access programming but agree[ing] with commenters that awarding grants to individuals 
is not an efficient use of PEGPETIA funds.”). The Authority also noted that 
Equipment purchased by individuals is not broadly available to the public or 
programming community and, therefore, has a much more limited impact. 
In addition, individual grants impose administrative burdens with respect to 
auditing and compliance. Importantly, PEG studios are required to maintain 
video production equipment and to make the equipment available to 
programmers. 
The Authority believes that the goals of the Act are best achieved by 
increasing the availability, quantity, and quality of equipment at local studios 
so that the greatest number of individuals have the ability to produce 
programming utilizing state of the art equipment and facilities. 
Revised Guidelines Decision, pp. 2–3 (citing General Statutes § 16-331a(b) and Conn. 
Agencies Regs. § 16-331a-11). 
The Authority’s concerns, as expressed in the Revised Guidelines Decision, are 
similarly applicable to providing PEG funding to individual PEG programmer organizations 
whose central mission is not producing television content. Many non-studio organizations 
received large amounts of funding in the past few grant cycles and provided compliance 
showing little to no programming provided to local access channels. Meanwhile, grants 
provided to PEG studios resulted in significantly more programming for local access 
channels. The Authority recognizes that some non-studio grant recipients provided more 
content to local access channels, however, those appear to be exceptions to the typical 
results. 
Accordingly, for this grant cycle, a cap for funding for PEG studios at $49,000 and 
for PEG programmers at $10,000 is appropriate. Table 5, below, provides the specific 
grant awarded to each eligible PEG Grant recipient.

As a result of the cap on PEG Grants, some recipients may need to adjust or scale 
down their original project plans and complete a smaller version of the proposed project. 
Authority approval is not required for adjustments to the itemized budget, bids, quotes, or 
estimates regarding quantity, brand, vendor, or other minor changes necessary for PEG

G. 
FUTURE GRANT CYCLES 
In the future, the Authority intends to administer PEGPETIA grant funds in a 
biennial docket. The lengthened grant cycles will provide several benefits, including (1) 
providing grant recipients with additional time to complete projects and demonstrate 
compliance with Authority orders, (2) allowing the Authority to better allocate funding to 
PEG Grant applicants with a demonstrated record of producing PEG programming for the 
community access channels, (3) allowing the Authority to place higher caps on grant 
awards, and (4) reducing the administrative burden on applicants associated with annual 
applications and compliance. 
A biennial docket allows for a longer grant cycle, in which recipients have nearly a 
year to use grant funding and comply with the Authority’s orders. In turn, the Authority 
and docket participants can review compliance filings to ensure completeness and 
determine eligibility for future grant awards before a new docket is opened. That timing 
will allow for greater accountability, particularly with respect to how much PEG 
programming is produced and provided to community access channels using PEG Grant 
funds. The Authority anticipates that PEG Grant recipients will make capital investments 
in the months following disbursement of funds, allowing for sufficient time to produce and 
submit programming to the community access channels before the compliance deadline. 
Accordingly, the Authority will have sufficient information to allocate funding to promote 
and improve public, educational, and governmental programming.

The Authority anticipates that recent reductions in the funding available in recent 
dockets will continue as cable subscriptions continue to decline. Allocating grant funds 
every other year will allow sufficient PEGPETIA funds to accumulate for recipients to 
undertake meaningful investments using grant funds. In addition, the amount of available 
funding would be known at the start of each proceeding, allowing applicants to more 
accurately plan to use allocated funding. 
Finally, the total amount of available funding would remain unaffected by the length 
of the grant cycle, which would allow grant recipients to receive the same funding but 
apply (and comply) half as often. The application window could also be shortened, 
permitting the Authority and docket participants more time in which to review applications 
for eligibility (and potentially allow grant applicants a larger window of time in which to 
correct deficiencies in their applications).
